data.title: Legends attached to the localities of Hradište and Koscelisko
data.excerpt: Three legends are attached to the localities of Hradište and Koscelisko in the northern Váh region: a shepherd and a wild he-goat beside a burnt-down hillfort, a wedding party drowned in the quagmire of Jezero, and a shadow that forbade a bold man ever to return to Zámčiská. Peter Schreiber reads the recurring motif of the devil as a possible demonisation of these places.
data.metaDescription: Three legends attached to the localities of Hradište and Koscelisko in the northern Váh region, recorded by Milan Húževka in Púchovské povesti.

children.text: We are bringing you the second part of the previous article, which concerned the presumed ancient road in the northern Váh region (Mariková, Mostište, Zbora). The author is once again Mgr. Peter Schreiber.

Three legends are also attached to the localities of Hradište and Koscelisko, which were recorded and published by Milan Húževka in the book Púchovské povesti (Legends of Púchov) and in the monograph on the village of Mestečko (Ján Mišún and colleagues). Below I give an abridged transcription of the legends.
The legend of the shepherd from below Čechovec[1]:
The legend relates that a certain herdsman, a shepherd, while hunting wild goats on a hill not far from the burnt-down
hillfort

, was met by a wild he-goat, which promised the shepherd that it would grant him one wish if he would not shoot the goats in its herd. Thereupon the he-goat gave him one of its horns, and the shepherd was to make a trumpet out of it. He was to sound the trumpet when things were at their worst for him, and one wish would be granted to him (Húževka 1990).
The legend of the drowned wedding party:
A young man from Mestečko was looking for a bride. Already as a little boy he used to pasture cattle at
Hradište

. He set his eye on a bride from the hamlet of Gaškov, above the village of Vydrná. One day a wayfarer passing across the pasture advised him to take her as his wife despite his father's prohibitions. He went courting across a place that was called
Jezero

. It was a place where more than one head of cattle had drowned. He knew how to avoid that dangerous place. When the time for the betrothal came, the young man called on the matchmakers to set out with him to Gaškov to ask for the bride. At midnight the bride together with the bridegroom had to set out for Mestečko. They went in the direction of
Jezero

, but the wild driver, as though he had underestimated the danger, drove the horses on. The carefree wedding guests were singing, the music was playing and the team drove straight into the quagmire of
Jezero

. At its edge the driver turned into the devil, the wayfarer who had once whispered the plan to the young man. The wagon found itself in the mud. At that moment the cockerel that the bridal attendant was carrying as a gift into the son-in-law's yard crowed. They all drowned in
Jezero

. During the night of St John, it is said, the singing of the wedding guests, the sounds of musical instruments and the crowing of a cockerel can be heard at the place. Note: according to the account of Katarína Václavíková (Mišún 2006).
The legend of Zámčiská:

Below the hill of Stráža an old koscel (church) is said to have stood. The people of Zbora called this place Koscel and the people of Mestečko Zámčiská. Strange things used to happen at Zámčiská and no one dared to go there at night. One bold man is said to have once waited at Zámčiská until midnight. When the watchman sounded the twelfth hour in Zbora, he became frightened. Then the ground moved beneath him, and nearby in the bank something cracked. Out of the crevice, between the roots of the beeches, the shadow of a man appeared, and it said to him: “never come here again”. This is a place that must not be desecrated. Anyone among ordinary people who came here could bring about immense misfortune. Note: according to the account of Ondrej Ševela (Mišún 2006).
Conclusion:

Two legends are attached to the locality of Hradište, in which supernatural forces are mentioned. The motif of the devil appears here; purely theoretically, this may be a demonisation of this place, just as in the case of the nearby locality of Jezero. In the adjacent part of Moravia, the Vsetín area, this question has been worked out in detail on the basis of archaeological sites of the early medieval period in connection with the oral tradition of the region (Hlavica 2009).

items.text: [1] The hamlet of Čechovec forms part of the village of Dohňany, the Zbora district.
[2] Jazerka, mentioned in the second text, “Šimúnky (Široká), Hradište, Koscelisko – možné súvislosti” (Šimúnky (Široká), Hradište, Koscelisko – possible links).
